Mapping STI activities across international organisations: 2026 snapshot from a new STIP Compass portal

Authors: Daniela Valenzuela and Jovana Poznan

Date: 31-07-2026
Data Story — STIP Compass — EC/OECD

International organisations play important roles in shaping science, technology and innovation (STI) systems. They support international co-operation, produce harmonised data on STI activities and performance, and provide policy advice and support to national STI systems. Information on the landscape of these STI-related activities remains difficult to navigate, since it is spread across many organisations, websites, mandates, and reporting systems, often using different terminology and classifications. This makes it hard for countries, international organisations and other stakeholders to see which organisations are doing what, where activities overlap, and where gaps or opportunities for collaboration may exist.

To fill this void, the OECD and European Commission have leveraged their joint STIP Compass infrastructure to launch a new beta mapping of more than 200 STI-related activities across 12 international organisations. This mapping, the results of which have been collected into a new portal, aims to improve transparency on the STI-related activities of international organisations, help identify potential overlaps and gaps, and support mutual learning and co-ordination.

What the data show

Across their STI-related activities, international organisations mainly generate intelligence and enable co-ordination — but do so through markedly different institutional configurations

A few common functions dominate the STI-related activities of international organisations. These include providing policy advice, supporting international collaboration, monitoring and data collection, and capacity building, which together account for a large majority of reported activities across the 12 participating organisations. The policy advice function alone is present in around one in three activities and used by every organisation participating in the mapping, while funding is offered by only a small proportion of activities in a small subset of organisations. International organisations' distinctive contribution therefore lies in producing and organising evidence, building institutional capability and facilitating exchange between countries, rather than in providing direct financial support to STI systems. This enabling role, however, is exercised quite differently depending on the international organisation's mandate: for example, the OECD's activities concentrate on standard setting and policy advice, in keeping with its role as a provider of comparative evidence and international standards, while UNESCO's activities show a markedly more diversified profile, with capacity building particularly prominent, reflecting its emphasis on norm diffusion and national capability strengthening.

The mix of support mechanisms differs between recently launched and long-standing activities, with policy intelligence as the one constant across both

Nearly a third of all activities were launched in the past five years, and close to a quarter date back more than two decades—the two most represented periods in the mapping data. The mechanisms used by STI-related activities differ markedly between periods: recent activities more often use policy intelligence, capacity building, and networking or collaborative platforms, while long-standing activities rely more on standards and certification and on research and technology infrastructure support. Policy intelligence is the one mechanism prominent across both. These differences most likely reflect key characteristics of some of these instruments and the ways in which international organisations are funded.

Go to section 3.2Figure 3Figure 4

STI-related activities span the full R&D and innovation chain, with applied research most targeted

Among activities for which data was collected, applied research is the most targeted point in the innovation chain by a clear margin, followed by technology and innovation diffusion, experimental development, and technology deployment at broadly similar levels, with basic research comparatively less prominent. This confirms that IOs’ STI-related activities span the whole innovation chain, with some bias towards translating and spreading existing knowledge rather than supporting fundamental discovery.

Go to section 3.6Figure 8Figure 9

Firms, investors and other market-facing actors remain markedly under-represented as target groups and beneficiaries across activities

Across the target group field, as well as in the system linkages and support mechanisms recorded for each activity, firms, SMEs, entrepreneurs and private investors feature far less often as beneficiaries than government entities, research and education organisations, or other international organisations. This pattern is consistent with the public-interest mandates of most participating organisations, but it also merits attention, since innovation development, deployment, diffusion and scaling typically depend on private capital, technology transfer and market adoption.

About the beta portal

Developed as part of the EC-OECD STIP Compass infrastructure, with support from UN DESA and the Interagency Task Team on STI for the SDGs (IATT) network, the beta portal contains more than 200 activities reported by 12 participating international organisations: ECLAC, IEA, ITU, NEA, OECD, OEI, UN DESA, UNECE, UNEP, UNESCO, WHO and WIPO. Further organisations and activities are expected to be added in future iterations.

This Data Story: (1) explains why the portal was developed; (2) describes the data model created with participating international organisations; (3) features and presents selected data analysis, including the patterns and potential gaps in STI-related activities revealed by the data, and considers the value of the portal for international organisation officials, government policy analysts and researchers; and (4) outlines next steps for expanding coverage and enriching the evidence base.

1. Why develop a portal on STI-related activities from international organisations?

International organisations (IOs) are engaged in various types of STI-related activities, but information about these is spread across many organisations, websites, mandates, and reporting systems, often using different terminology and classifications. The Portal on STI Activities of IOs seeks to make this information more findable and coherent, bringing together harmonised information on relevant activities into a single evidence base. The beta version of the portal maps activities from 12 IOs and highlights how they support STI across a range of fields. While not yet a comprehensive map of the global ecosystem of international organisations’ STI-related activities, the portal represents an important first step towards greater transparency, mutual learning, and collaboration. By providing a central repository of information, it helps IOs, national governments, and researchers identify potential synergies in an increasingly complex international STI landscape.

2. What information does the portal collect?

2.1. Unit of data collection and analysis

Different from the STIP Compass general website that collects information on STI policy initiatives from national governments, the new IOs’ STI Portal uses ‘activities’ as the unit of data collection and analysis. It should be noted that not all activities implemented by IOs are included in this portal; rather, only major activities demonstrating continuity are captured.

Definition of an STI Activity

An STI-related activity refers to any initiative, programme, policy, or project undertaken by an international organisation that supports or promotes science, technology, and innovation. These activities can vary widely depending on the organisation’s mandate, sector, and geographic scope. Activities may involve multiple support mechanisms and multiple direct beneficiaries. Minor administrative actions and isolated events are excluded.

2.2. Data model or taxonomy

Data collection and analysis require structures to organise information. These structures are provided by data models, which define the variables, categories and relationships needed to classify and manage data consistently. The grouping of information into agreed categories is known as a taxonomy. Together, data models and taxonomies support systematic data collection and provide a common language for reporting and analysis.

The data model for developing the IOs portal was developed through an iterative process combining desk research, adaptation to the IOs context, and consultation with participating organisations.

The desk research started from the OECD STIP Compass taxonomy, which provides a structured approach for classifying science, technology and innovation policy initiatives from national governments. This taxonomy was reviewed and adapted to reflect the specific nature of IOs’ activities, which often differ from national policy initiatives in their mandates, audiences, delivery mechanisms and levels of intervention. The review also considered relevant previous mapping exercises, including the IATT-STI Mapping Sub-Group’s 2017 exercise, which collected around 1,600 UN activities related to STI from 20 UN agencies, as well as GOSPIN from UNESCO which contains relevant classifications of IOs. This helped identify additional elements needed to capture the breadth and heterogeneity of STI-related activities across the international system.

Consultations were then carried out with multiple IOs during 2025 through workshops, one-to-one interviews and written feedback. These consultations tested whether the proposed categories were understandable, usable in a questionnaire format and sufficiently flexible to describe different types of STI-related activities.

This process produced a proposed data model and taxonomy for classifying IO STI-related activities. The model comprises a structured set of fields and response options designed to capture key information on each initiative, combining categorical classifications with open-text fields. It aims to provide sufficient detail for analysis while remaining practical and manageable for organisations to complete. As the model is being tested through this project, future versions may be revised based on implementation experience and further feedback.

The version used in the beta portal is available in the document: IOs activities taxonomy proposal - final version.pdf.

Understanding the data model

Three taxonomic dimensions structure the data model, each characterising a different aspect of an STI-related activity.

Activity roles/functions

What IOs do to support STI systems. Organisations report activities across eight functional roles: policy advice, standard setting, monitoring and data, international collaboration, capacity building, awareness and advocacy, ethics and responsible innovation, and funding.

Support mechanisms

How IOs support STI systems. The model includes 18 support mechanisms organised into five categories: governance, direct financial support, collaborative infrastructures, guidance, regulation and standardisation, and capacity building, support and incentives.

Direct beneficiaries

Who benefits directly from IO support to STI systems. The model includes 31 beneficiary types organised into nine categories spanning government entities, research and education organisations, firms and groups in civic society.

Additional fields capture the level of engagement, alignment with the Sustainable Development Goals, position along the R&D and innovation stages, types of linkages supported in the STI system, partner and donor organisations, budget range and evaluation status. Open-text fields capture contextual information, including description, objectives, background, institutional mandate and expected impact.

The fiche and detailed taxonomy are at the bottom of this data story.

How was the data collected?

Data was collected through a structured survey distributed directly to participating IOs between late 2025 and mid-2026. In total, 203 initiatives were reported across 12 organisations. The number of initiatives submitted varied considerably, ranging from 4 to 29 per organisation.

As this was a pilot exercise, such variation largely reflects the limited scope of the initial data collection effort rather than differences in overall levels of STI-related activity. Future iterations are expected to expand the coverage of initiatives and support a more comprehensive mapping across participating organisations.

3. Main insights from the data collected

The dataset enables a wide range of mappings and analyses. It can be used to map specific fields, including functional roles, support mechanisms, target groups, levels of govenance, STI system linkages, and activities across the R&D and innovation chain. These mappings make it possible to assess the prominence and relative distribution of each category, as well as how widely they are represented across participating IOs. The data also support comparative analysis across IOs, revealing differences in the composition of their activity portfolios. Temporal mapping is possible through the start dates of activities, allowing analysis of both the distribution of activities over time and the use of different instruments across periods. In addition, open-text fields enable topic analysis to identify the substantive areas of work covered by IOs’ activities. The analysis below explores the data from these different perspectives to build a clearer picture of IOs’ work in STI, including common patterns, organisational profiles, and potential gaps.

3.1. The role of international organisations

International organisations perform a range of roles that support STI systems. They advise governments, produce and organise evidence, develop common standards, strengthen institutional capabilities and the skills of individuals, facilitate international co-operation, raise awareness of STI issues, support the responsible governance of emerging technologies and, in some cases, provide funding.

Figure 1 provides an overview of this functional landscape by showing both how frequently each role appears across the activity portfolio and how widely it is used across the participating organisations.

The distribution of functions shows that IOs most often perform policy advice and other knowledge- and capability-based roles. Policy advice appears in around one-third of all activities and across all 12 participating organisations. It includes support to countries in developing, strengthening and implementing STI policies through analytical studies, evidence-based assessments, strategic frameworks and policy-design activities. Reflecting a core function of IOs’ engagement with member countries, this role helps governments to establish STI priorities, improve the effectiveness of policy interventions, and build governance frameworks that foster innovation-driven economic and social development.

Capacity building, international collaboration, and monitoring and data each feature in around one-quarter of activities, illustrating how IOs support STI systems beyond policy formulation. Capacity-building activities strengthen the skills, institutional capabilities and operational arrangements required to design and implement STI policies and programmes. International collaboration expands access to knowledge, resources and expertise through science diplomacy, policy dialogue, collaborative research and cross-border innovation networks. Complementing these efforts, monitoring and data activities provide the evidence base for effective STI governance through indicators, databases, scoreboards, and measurement frameworks and benchmarking tools that enable countries to track progress, identify emerging trends, and refine policy interventions over time.

A further set of roles helps shape the wider institutional and normative environment for STI. Awareness and advocacy and standard setting each appear in just over one in five activities. Awareness and advocacy raise the visibility of STI issues, while standard setting contributes to the development of shared norms, guidelines, and technical frameworks that support international co-operation and interoperability. Ethics and responsible Innovation address the governance of emerging technologies through principles, frameworks, and tools that encourage responsible innovation, public engagement, and anticipatory approaches to technological change. Funding stands apart as the least common functional role, appearing in fewer than one in twenty activities and across only four participating organisations. Where present, it includes grants, loans, fellowships and other financial instruments supporting research, skills, infrastructure or innovation. Its limited presence suggests that IOs contribute more often by strengthening the enabling conditions for STI through policy advice, evidence production, capacity building, international co-operation and common standards than through direct financial support.

Despite common areas of activity, organisations exhibit distinct functional profiles reflecting their mandates and areas of expertise. Some organisations maintain a relatively balanced portfolio across multiple roles, while others display a strong concentration in specific functions. Figure 2 examines these differences by showing the share of each organisation’s reported activities associated with each functional role.

For instance, the OECD’s STI activities are concentrated on standard setting, policy advice and monitoring and data, reflecting its role as a provider of evidence-based policy analysis, international standards and comparative indicators. In contrast, UNESCO displays a broader footprint, with strong engagement in capacity building, international collaboration and policy advice, consistent with its emphasis on global co-operation, norm diffusion and strengthening national STI capacities. WHO’s STI activities span across ethics and responsibility, capacity building, international collaboration, and monitoring and data, reflecting its role in developing global health norms, supporting national health systems and facilitating international responses to emerging technological and public health challenges. WIPO exhibits a distinctive profile characterised by a strong focus on monitoring and data, capacity building and intellectual property-related policy advice, consistent with its mandate to support innovation ecosystems, intellectual property governance and evidence-based policymaking. Overall, the distribution of roles in IOs’ STI activities reflects their respective institutional mandates and areas of expertise, with similar patterns observed across the broader set of organisations.

3.2. How do IOs deliver their activities and has this changed over time?

Support mechanisms show how IOs turn broad STI roles into concrete forms of implementation. While roles describe what IOs seek to do, such as advising governments, producing data or supporting collaboration, support mechanisms capture the instruments through which they deliver this work. These range from governance arrangements, convening bodies and strategic agendas to policy intelligence, standards, collaborative platforms, technical assistance and, in some cases, direct financial support. Analysing these mechanisms helps show whether IOs mainly support STI systems by producing evidence, building capacity, connecting actors, shaping rules or providing resources.

The distribution of activities over time provides an overview of when the IOs activities were established. Temporal mapping, based on the start dates of activities, makes it possible to trace patterns of development. As shown in Figure 3, the activity portfolio is concentrated in two periods: recently launched activities and long-standing activities. Almost a third of all activities started between 2021 and 2025, making this period the one with the highest number of activities. At the same time, nearly a quarter pre-date 2001, suggesting a core of institutionalised, long-standing activities that have persisted for decades.

An interesting question is whether and how the instruments used by IOs have changed over time. Figure 4 focuses on the two most prominent periods for start dates of activities in the dataset and maps the instruments they use. The Y-axis shows activities that started between 2021 and 2025, while the X-axis shows activities that started before 2001. Instruments positioned above the diagonal line have a relatively higher share in the recent period, whereas those below the line are more strongly represented among activities launched before 2001.

The chart shows that policy intelligence, capacity building, networking platforms, and consultations and forums are more common among recently established activities. While this might suggest a growing popularity of these instruments – perhaps reflecting a growing emphasis on knowledge sharing, stakeholder engagement, and support functions within the international STI landscape – these patterns should be read with care. This is because activities using these sorts of instruments are more likely to be subject to “churn”, meaning they are more frequently started and discontinued after a few years than activities using other instruments. This may be because these activities are set up to meet emerging and sometimes fast-moving needs and/or the requirements of short-to-medium-term funding streams. This hypothesis is supported by two other observations in the data. First, instruments that are strongly associated with activities launched before 2001 reflect more stable and long-standing modes of delivery, including legal instruments, standards and certification, and support for technology and research infrastructure. Second, the fewer activities reported in between (i.e., between 2001-15 – see Figure 3) likely reflects the discontinuation of initiatives following the normal lifecycle of short-term, project-based funding.

3.3. What are the main target groups of IOs activities?

Looking at the target groups of IO activities reveals how international organisations engage with STI systems, and where their reach is more limited. As intergovernmental entities, international organisations primarily engage with national governments, which are the target group in around four out of five STI activities (Figure 5). This reflects the central role that IOs play in supporting public policy through policy advice, capacity building, data collection and analysis, standard setting, regulatory frameworks, and international co-operation.

Beyond national governments, the next most prominent target groups are IOs themselves and the research community. More than half also target established researchers, public research institutes and higher education institutions, while academies, academic societies and early-career researchers also feature prominently. This suggests that IOs engage STI systems mainly through public institutions, scientific communities and knowledge infrastructures.

By contrast, firms, SMEs, entrepreneurs and private investors appear much less often as direct target groups. This pattern reflects the mandates of many IOs, which focus primarily on governments, research systems and public-interest functions rather than direct market intermediation. However, since firms and investors often play central roles in innovation and technology development, scaling and diffusion, this finding points to a gap in IOs’ portfolios that they may need to examine.

3.4. At what level of governance does IOs’ STI-related activities engage?

The dataset also reveals whether IOs’ STI-related activities primarily operate as supranational co-ordination mechanisms, country-level support tools, or more targeted interventions in specific local contexts. As shown in Figure 6, activities are strongly concentrated at the international level, appearing in more than nine out of ten activities. This reflects the distinctive role of IOs in convening countries, producing comparative evidence, sharing good practices, developing common frameworks and supporting co-ordination across borders. The national level also features prominently, with around three fifths of activities directed towards country-level engagement, such as policy reviews, technical assistance, capacity building or support for national STI strategies. By contrast, local-level engagement appears much less frequently, at around one in ten activities, which is consistent with the fact that many IOs work primarily through national governments or international platforms rather than directly with cities, communities or local institutions.

3.5. What linkages do IOs support in the STI system?

The performance of innovation systems is strongly influenced by the linkages between different actors, notably firms, public research, government and society at large. Innovation systems may underperform because of weaknesses in these linkages, with ‘system failures’ often providing strong rationales for policy intervention. International organisations exist, in part, to address co-ordination problems that individual countries, firms or research actors cannot easily resolve alone. Support to linkages therefore captures the connections that IO activities seek to build or strengthen in STI systems. These include promoting sustained collaboration, convening spaces, shared standards, policy learning and cross-border knowledge exchange.

The analysis of these linkages shown in Figure 7 reveals that IOs mainly support broad, system-level linkages. Linkages across sectors or policy domains, between science and society, and among research organisations and research fields are among the most prominent. The comparatively lower emphasis on linkages involving firms and entrepreneurs is in line with the analysis above (section 3.3), pointing to relatively weak engagement with the private sector. Given the critical roles of these actors in transforming knowledge into new technologies and services, and in supporting their wider diffusion throughout the economy and society, IOs could give greater attention to their linkages in STI systems.

3.6. How do IOs’ STI-related activities map across the R&D and innovation chain?

Technological innovation is understood as a complex process involving a range of actors – notably firms, investors, universities and regulators – engaged in a mix of activities, including basic and applied research, experimental development, and technology demonstration, deployment and diffusion. These activities can be modelled into an “innovation chain” in which each is juxtaposed. This model can be useful for mapping innovation-related activities, the links between them, and any significant gaps, including so-called ‘valleys of death’ where, for example, the translation of research and experimental development into technology demonstration can be weak. In this way, the innovation chain model is useful for policy makers – and by extension, for international organisations – to identify points in the innovation process where they could usefully intervene.

Figure 8 maps the share of IOs’ STI-related activities against different points in the innovation chain. It shows that approximately three in four activities map to support for applied research. Support for diffusion, experimental development and deployment follows at broadly comparable levels, each targeted by close to three in five activities, with demonstration somewhat lower, at around one in two. Basic research is targeted by under half of the activities mapped. This distribution indicates that IOs are engaged across the full innovation process, but with a distinct centre of gravity: their activity is oriented less towards fundamental discovery and more towards the application, testing and diffusion of existing knowledge, consistent with a systems-oriented role centred on translation and adoption rather than upstream research.

This systems-oriented profile, however, is not evenly distributed across organisations, as Figure 9 illustrates by disaggregating the same distribution by organisation: individual organisations tend to specialise at particular points in the chain rather than covering it in full. Organisations such as the IEA and the OECD concentrate on experimental development, demonstration and deployment, consistent with a focus on technology transition and policy implementation. UNESCO, by contrast, concentrates on applied research and diffusion, with a more limited presence at the intermediate translation stages, reflecting a profile centred on knowledge generation and dissemination rather than deployment support.

3.7. What substantive topic areas do IOs’ STI-related activities cover?

STI as a field is crosscutting and horizontal, covering a range of challenges, policy domains, and industrial sectors. Open-text fields in the portal’s dataset can be analysed to identify the substantive domains covered by IOs’ STI activities. A topic-based analysis of activity descriptions, objectives, expected impacts, examples and background information identified eight broad topic domains across the 203 STI activities. Each activity was assigned to the domain with the strongest textual evidence, using a keyword and phrase-based scoring approach. Figure 10 reports each domain’s share of total activities, the number of participating IOs, and the total number of activities.

The analysis points to two broad types of domains. The first consists of cross-cutting areas with both relatively high activity volumes and participation from several IOs. These include STI systems, sustainability and policy transformation; digital, data and connectivity; and education, skills and inclusion. Their prominence suggests that these domains act as shared foundations for IO activities in STI, reflecting broad policy concerns that cut across organisational mandates.

The second type consists of more specialised domains, including clean energy and industrial decarbonisation; intellectual property and knowledge assets; health systems and digital health; and nuclear science, safety and skills. These domains involve fewer IOs, likely reflecting mandate-driven specialisation, where activity is concentrated among organisations with specific responsibilities, technical capacities or sectoral remits.

Looking ahead: further enriching the evidence base

Looking ahead, the portal is expected to expand both in terms of participating organisations and its data coverage. The survey underpinning the data collection is envisaged to be conducted on a biennial basis, enabling regular updates with new evidence and insights. Several IOs have already engaged in the initial phases of the project – through consultations, and the shaping of the data model – and represent a strong foundation for broadening participation in future iterations.

The portal marks an important step towards making the collective STI engagement of IOs more visible, comparable and actionable. As the evidence base grows, it has the potential to support more informed co-ordination and strategic alignment across the international landscape. It can serve as a practical resource for officials within IOs seeking synergies and partnerships, for government stakeholders aiming to better navigate and leverage international support, and for researchers and analysts examining the evolving architecture of global STI governance.

On the 8 July 2026 the portal was launched jointly between the OECD, the EC and UNESCO. You can watch the recording here: Launch of a new portal on the STI activities of international organisations

Detailed taxonomy

Functional themes: what the activity does+
Theme/RoleDefinition
Policy adviceSupport to countries in developing and strengthening STI policies, including policy analysis, analytical studies, strategy development, policy design and implementation support.
Standard settingActivities that establish or promote international norms, guidelines, protocols and technical standards for STI, research practices, data interoperability, safety or technology governance.
FundingFinancial mechanisms to support public research, business R&D, technological development, talent and human capital. Instruments may include grants, centres of excellence, loans, credits, equity finance, fellowships or student loans.
Capacity buildingActivities that build human and organisational capabilities in STI and STI policy. This can include training, mentoring, stronger institutional routines and improved organisational practices for researchers, policy professionals, intermediaries and firms.
International collaborationActivities that facilitate international STI co-operation, science diplomacy, collaborative research, research and innovation networks, policy dialogue, technology transfer or co-operation mechanisms.
Monitoring and dataData collection and analysis activities, including indicators, reporting frameworks, databases, dashboards and scoreboards.
Ethics and responsible research and innovationFrameworks, principles or tools that support responsible research and innovation, public engagement and anticipatory governance in emerging technologies such as AI, synthetic biology, neurotechnology or quantum.
Awareness and advocacyCampaigns, reports, multilateral processes or stakeholder engagement efforts that raise awareness of how STI can contribute to global challenges.
Support mechanisms: how the activity is delivered+
Governance+
MechanismDefinition
Strategies, agendas and plansStrategic documents developed by IOs to outline visions, priorities and frameworks for STI support. They may guide the organisation's work, shape international efforts or inform member states' national STI policies.
Convening bodies and collaboration mechanismsInstitutional arrangements, committees, advisory bodies or co-ordination frameworks supported by IOs to guide STI policy and governance, improve policy coherence or support joint action among IOs.
SecretariatsAdministrative bodies established under IO protocols or treaties to support the operation of multilateral STI-related agreements or funding mechanisms.
Stakeholder consultation and expert forumsProcesses initiated by IOs to engage stakeholders and experts in dialogue, consensus building or policy advice on STI issues.

Public research fundingDirect financial support to public research institutions, including institutional block grants, competitive projects and support for core research functions or centres of excellence.

Talent developmentFinancial support for individuals pursuing education or research careers in science and innovation-related fields, including fellowships, scholarships and student loans.

Science and technology soft lawNon-legally binding guidelines, recommendations, frameworks and tools developed by an IO for new technologies or science practices.

Entrepreneurs and investorsConnections between entrepreneurial actors and sources of finance.
Across sectors or policy domainsConnections across policy areas, sectors or domains of public action.
Science and societyConnections between scientific actors and society.
Whole innovation ecosystemsSupport for broader ecosystem-level connections and co-ordination.
Not relevantUsed when the activity does not support an STI system linkage.
Level of engagement+
OptionDescription
InternationalActivities that enable international STI support or co-operation.
NationalActivities that support national governments or national STI systems.
LocalActivities supporting STI at a local level.
R&D and innovation stages+
OptionDescription
Basic researchExperimental or theoretical work to acquire new knowledge of underlying phenomena and observable facts, without a specific application in view.
Applied researchOriginal investigation to acquire new knowledge, directed mainly towards a specific practical aim or objective.
Experimental developmentSystematic work using research and practical experience to produce additional knowledge, new products or processes, or improvements to existing ones.
DemonstrationOperation or testing of a prototype or pilot in realistic conditions to evidence performance.
DeploymentIntroduction of an innovation into use, either as a product made available to users or markets, or as a process brought into organisational use.
DiffusionSpread and adoption of an innovation by other units, including adoption of a product or process developed elsewhere.
Phase-outManaged withdrawal of an implemented innovation from use or the market.
Not relevantUsed when the R&D and innovation chain does not apply.

OptionDescription
1. No povertyEnd poverty in all its forms everywhere
2. Zero hungerEnd hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture
3. Good health and well-beingEnsure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages
4. Quality educationEnsure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all
5. Gender equalityAchieve gender equality and empower all women and girls
6. Clean water and sanitationEnsure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
7. Affordable and clean energyEnsure access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy for all
8. Decent work and economic growthPromote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all
9. Industry, innovation and infrastructureBuild resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialisation and foster innovation
10. Reduced inequalitiesReduce inequality within and among countries
11. Sustainable cities and communitiesMake cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable
12. Responsible consumption and productionEnsure sustainable consumption and production patterns
13. Climate actionTake urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts
14. Life below waterConserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources for sustainable development
15. Life on landProtect, restore and promote sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests, combat desertification, halt land degradation and halt biodiversity loss
16. Peace, justice and strong institutionsPromote peaceful and inclusive societies, provide access to justice and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions
17. Partnerships for the goalsStrengthen implementation and revitalise the global partnership for sustainable development

Target geography+
OptionDescription
Country selectorIndividual countries can be selected from a country list.
ContinentsActivities may target whole regions such as Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Oceania or South America.
Organisation groupingsThe model includes groupings such as OECD member countries, OECD partner economies and UN member states.
